newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Government to remove GAN insurance head.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Government to remove GAN insurance head.

text.p: The French government will fire the chairman of state-owned insurer GAN next week if he continues to resist a call for his departure after a failed bid to privatise GAN banking subsidiary CIC, a government source said on Tuesday.
"There will be a decree ending his mandate," the government source said, after GAN (Groupe des Assurances Nationales) confirmed Jean-Jacques Bonnaud was not resigning.

This was standard procedure in the case where the head of a state company would not resign, and the decree removing him would be adopted at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday of next week, where a replacement was likely to be named, the source said.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said last Thursday that he was scrapping a tender to privatise Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC), after getting only one eligible offer, from Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP).

The decision to demand Bonnaud's departure was announced by the finance ministry on Monday in agreement with Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who crossed swords with Bonnaud in February over an attempt by Juppe to place a close advisor at the head of CIC.
Juppe backed down after his attempt to place Pierre-Mathieu Duhamel sparked a storm of controversy over the government's role in appointments at state companies.
Bonnaud subsequently named Bernard Yoncourt head of CIC, but a source said whoever replaced Bonnaud would name a successor to Yoncourt.
Yoncourt infuriated Arthuis in October after declaring on television, in the middle of the privatisation tender process, that a sale to a major French bank could spell "death" for CIC.
CIC is a group of 11 regional banks whose main forte is its strong local position and relations with a clientele of large and medium sized corporations.
Arthuis described Yoncourt's remarks as "unacceptable" and threatened to "draw the consequences".
The irritation showed through again last week when Arthuis announced the scrapping of the sell-off tender and broke from his usually guarded rhetoric to criticise Bonnaud and Yoncourt.
"The managers of GAN and CIC did not behave in a way to encourage progress in this process," he said at the time.

The government received only two bids for CIC -- from BNP and Societe Generale. The French privatisation commission rejected Societe Generale's offer as it did not comply with terms imposed by the government, of which the most important is that any buyer must preserve the bank's regional integrity.
Arthuis said he was determined to privatise the group but that he was breaking off a tender in which there was only one eligible offer on the table to take more time to reflect.

Staff and trade unions opposed the sell-off (which had been seen as a prerequisite to selling GAN itself) with strikes and protests over feared job losses. The spectre of a break-up of the group also sparked widespread fears among local politicians.

Banking analysts said the strict government conditions on the sale could only attract a low-price offer for CIC, which was valued at around 14 billion francs ($2.75 billion) by GAN. That would correspond to about 9.4 billion francs for the 67 percent which the government had put up for sale.
